paragraphs: Cross Creek Programs was a boarding program for teenagers in La Verkin, Utah, that ran from 1988 to 2012 as part of the World Wide Association of Specialty Programs and Schools (WWASPS).{wiki,rtt} Robert Lichfield and Brent Facer founded it.{wiki} Former students have described violent restraint, isolation, deprivation and sexual abuse there for decades.{rtt,wiki} In 2006 one family's lawsuit against Cross Creek and WWASPS grew into one of the largest abuse cases against the network. By 2012 it had more than 350 former students and family members as plaintiffs.{ww,sp12}

Cross Creek opened in 1988 as a program for girls, Cross Creek Manor, and later added a boys' program, Cross Creek Center.{wiki} Lichfield had worked at Provo Canyon School. In 1999 he incorporated WWASPS with the lawyer Ralph Atkin, and Cross Creek became one of its programs.{wiki,reason} Its school, Cross Creek Academy (also called Browning Academy), was accredited by the Northwest Accreditation Commission, and Karr Farnsworth served as director.{wiki} Families paid about $4,495 a month. Boys usually stayed 16 to 18 months and girls 12 to 14.{rtt} As early as 1992 the program used an escort company to take teenagers from their homes to La Verkin.{wiki}

Survivors describe violent restraint and solitary confinement as punishment for minor rule breaks. They also describe food and sleep deprivation, being left outside in extreme temperatures, psychological abuse and sexual abuse.{rtt} In a 2021 Vice News report, graduates, parents and former staff called the program "manipulative, abusive and traumatic." They described a male staff member supervising a 13-year-old girl while she showered, and staff staging re-enactments of rapes. The program's executives denied the allegations.{wiki}

On August 25, 2006, William Chase Wood and his parents sued WWASPS, Cross Creek Center for Boys, Cross Creek Manor, Lichfield, Ken Kay, Farnsworth and others. They alleged physical, emotional and sexual abuse, confinement and forced labor during about two years at Cross Creek and High Impact, and racketeering in how the programs were sold to parents.{ww} By October 2006, 25 plaintiffs had joined.{wiki} The federal court dismissed the racketeering claims. In 2011 the case was refiled in state court on behalf of 350 former students and 150 parents, who alleged beatings, sexual abuse and being made to lie in urine and feces as punishment.{dn11,sp12} In 2012 it was moved to the Fifth District Court in St. George, where 38 of the 57 defendants lived.{sp12}

Cross Creek stayed open through the litigation. It later merged with Horizon Academy on the Cross Creek campus, and from 2012 it was marketed as Youth Foundation Inc.{rtt} It closed in 2012.{ach,wiki} Part of the site is now a motel, and the rest has been closed off and abandoned.{rtt}
